article_blocks.text: Strain Type: 80% Indica / 20% Sativa
Genetics: Super Skunk × White Widow
Breeder: Green House Seed Company
THC Content: 14–20%
CBD Content: 1–2%
Terpene Profile: Myrcene , alpha-humulene
Primary Flavors: Earth, sweet fruit, herbs, skunk, spice
Flowering Time (Indoor): 8–9 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: Late September to early October
Indoor Yield: 700–800 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: 900–1,000 g per plant
Grow Difficulty: Moderate

Great White Shark belongs to an era of cannabis breeding when resin production, physical potency, and unmistakable aroma mattered more than dessert-inspired strain names. Emerging from the famous Dutch breeding scene of the 1990s, this old-school hybrid combines the heavy structure and pungency of Super Skunk with genetics from the White Widow family , creating dense flowers that can appear almost dusted in frost by harvest.

The name may suggest aggression, but the experience is usually less frantic than formidable: a relatively clear beginning gradually sinks into substantial body relaxation that can linger for hours. Earth, herbs, sweet fruit, skunk, and spice form the flavor foundation, while thick trichome coverage gives the plant the visual character associated with classic “White” marijuana genetics. For consumers exploring historically important weed strains rather than the latest candy cross, Great White Shark remains an excellent example of the resin-heavy indica hybrids that helped define premium European cannabis during the late twentieth century.
Genetics and Lineage

Green House Seed Company created Great White Shark by combining Super Skunk with its famous White Widow genetic foundation. The breeder traditionally describes the complete ancestry as Super Skunk, Brazilian, and South Indian, reflecting the Brazilian and South Indian parents associated with White Widow. Super Skunk itself grew out of the Skunk family, pairing Skunk #1 characteristics with additional Afghan influence to create a plant with greater density, stronger physical effects, heavy resin production, and a penetrating sweet-skunk aroma. Bringing those qualities into the White Widow family intensified the indica side of the resulting hybrid without eliminating the more uplifting cerebral qualities inherited through its broader lineage.

White Widow is central to understanding the character of Great White Shark. The original White Widow became internationally famous for extreme trichome coverage, a potent mixture of cerebral and physical effects, and flowers carrying earthy, woody, herbal, and peppery aromas. Its Brazilian and South Indian ancestry introduced considerable genetic diversity, while selection focused strongly on resin production. Great White Shark takes that already resinous foundation and reinforces the heavier side of the plant through Super Skunk. Consequently, mature flowers often become compact and heavily coated while the effect shifts toward deeper physical relaxation than consumers might expect from White Widow alone.

The strain also belongs to the historically important “White” generation of cannabis varieties. Alongside cultivars such as White Russian and White Rhino , it helped establish the visual expectation that premium marijuana should display obvious resin glands across the flower and surrounding sugar leaves. Great White Shark gained recognition in cannabis competitions during the 1990s and 2000s, further establishing the genetics as more than a temporary commercial release. Decades later, the cultivar remains recognizable precisely because its combination of Skunk vigor, White-family resin, manageable flowering time, and strong body effects continues to offer qualities breeders still pursue.
Effects and Experience

Great White Shark does not usually begin with the immediate mental heaviness its indica dominance might suggest. The opening can feel surprisingly clean, with a mild cerebral lift, improved mood, and a sense that external distractions have become less demanding. There may be a brief period when conversation, music, television, or relaxed social activity remains appealing. That initial clarity is important because it distinguishes the experience from cultivars that become sedating almost immediately. The strain’s reputation for heaviness develops somewhat later, making dosage particularly important for anyone expecting to remain productive.

As the high matures, attention shifts steadily toward the body. Muscles can feel looser, limbs become heavier, and the desire to move unnecessarily often diminishes. At moderate levels, this physical component can feel deeply comfortable without completely shutting down mental activity. Larger amounts are another matter. Strong doses may produce substantial couch-lock, appetite stimulation, slower reaction time, and eventually sleepiness. The result is a classic indica-style progression in which mental ease gradually becomes physical weight rather than an abrupt knockout effect.

Even though contemporary cannabis routinely exceeds the THC percentages historically associated with Great White Shark, numerical potency does not tell the entire story. Cannabinoid ratios, terpene content, personal tolerance, consumption method, and dose all influence how strong flower feels. A well-grown example can remain surprisingly powerful despite appearing moderate on a laboratory label compared with modern 25–30% THC weed. Dry mouth and dry eyes are common possibilities, while excessive consumption may cause dizziness, anxiety, or temporary discomfort in THC-sensitive individuals. Evening use is generally the most natural fit.
Medical Benefits

The cultivar has long attracted medical marijuana consumers interested in substantial physical relaxation without immediately overwhelming mental effects. Chronic discomfort is one of the most commonly associated uses. THC can alter pain perception through the endocannabinoid system and other neurological pathways, while the heavy body effect may make persistent aches or muscular tension feel less intrusive. Great White Shark should not be considered a treatment for any specific condition, but its combination of cannabinoids and sedating properties helps explain why pain-focused cannabis consumers have historically shown interest in the strain.

Sleep can be another area where its characteristics are relevant. The later stage of the experience frequently becomes much heavier than the beginning, especially after larger doses. For people whose difficulty sleeping is associated with physical tension or an inability to relax at night, that progression may be useful. Appetite stimulation also occurs with many THC-rich cannabis varieties, and Great White Shark can produce noticeable hunger as the effects develop. Some medical consumers therefore explore similar strains when poor appetite or nausea is part of their symptom picture.

Its terpene chemistry adds additional complexity. Myrcene contributes much of the earthy, herbal aroma and is frequently found in cannabis cultivars associated with physical relaxation. Beta-caryophyllene produces peppery spice and is unusual because it can interact with CB2 receptors in the endocannabinoid system. Humulene contributes woody, earthy, hop-like characteristics. Research into how these terpenes influence the effects of whole cannabis flower is still developing, so their presence should not be treated as proof of a particular medical outcome. Individual response remains more important than a strain label.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Few aspects of Great White Shark feel particularly modern, and that is part of its appeal. The aroma is rooted in old-school cannabis: damp earth, dried herbs, skunk, wood, pepper, and resin. Sweetness appears around the edges rather than dominating the bouquet. Depending on phenotype and cultivation, that sweetness may resemble ripe fruit, mild citrus, or a sugary herbal character. Breaking apart a cured flower usually releases a stronger skunky note, followed by pepper and a deeper earthy smell inherited from the White Widow side.

Myrcene is commonly among the most prominent terpenes and reinforces the earthy, musky, herbal foundation. Alpha-humulene contributes dry wood, herbs, and an almost hop-like bitterness, while beta-caryophyllene adds black pepper and warm spice. Together they create a terpene profile considerably different from modern cannabis bred around candy, pastry, or tropical fruit aromas. There is sweetness, but it remains anchored to unmistakably pungent weed.

The flavor tends to begin earthy and mildly sweet before turning more herbal and spicy on the exhale. Some plants show a clearer fruity quality, whereas others lean heavily toward Skunk funk, wood, and pepper. Proper curing makes a large difference. Flowers dried too quickly can lose much of the underlying sweetness and become harsh or generically earthy. A slower controlled cure preserves the contrast between the sweeter Super Skunk influence and the deeper resinous characteristics of the White Widow family.
Growing Information

Great White Shark displays the compact, broad architecture expected from an indica-dominant hybrid. Plants usually remain manageable indoors while producing numerous lateral branches and a relatively bushy canopy. Those characteristics make the cultivar suitable for Sea of Green or Screen of Green systems, depending on plant count and vegetative time. Topping and low-stress training can also help distribute growth across multiple flowering sites. Because foliage can become thick, selective pruning is useful for improving light penetration and airflow through the center of the plant.

Indoor flowering generally takes eight to nine weeks. Green House has historically noted that extending maturity slightly can increase resin development and influence sweetness, although harvest timing should ultimately be determined from flower maturity rather than a calendar alone. Dense buds and heavy resin are major strengths of the plant, but dense flowers also require environmental control. Relative humidity should be watched carefully during late bloom, particularly when large colas begin closing their internal structure. Adequate airflow around and underneath the canopy reduces the risk of stagnant moisture.

Yield potential is one of the cultivar’s stronger cultivation characteristics. Optimized indoor gardens can approach roughly 700 to 800 grams per square meter, although actual results depend on lighting, genetics, vegetative duration, canopy management, nutrition, and environmental stability. Outdoors, well-established plants grown in strong sunlight with sufficient root volume may approach 900 to 1,000 grams per plant under exceptional conditions. Those figures represent potential rather than guaranteed production.

Outdoor plants generally mature from late September into early October in Northern Hemisphere climates. The plant can grow substantially wider outdoors than it does inside, building a branched structure capable of supporting considerable flower mass. Medium-to-heavy feeding can be tolerated when root health and environmental conditions are strong, but pushing nutrients simply because the cultivar can handle them is unnecessary. Maintaining healthy roots, adequate calcium and magnesium, steady irrigation, and good canopy airflow is more valuable than excessive fertilization. Resin production makes mature flowers attractive for traditional hash or other extraction applications as well as dried flower.
FAQ
Is Great White Shark an indica or sativa strain?

Great White Shark is generally described as approximately 80% indica and 20% sativa. Its growth structure and later effects strongly reflect the indica side, with compact branching, dense flowers, body relaxation, and potential sedation. Some cerebral clarity can remain early in the experience, however, preventing it from feeling like a purely one-dimensional indica.
What strains make Great White Shark?

Green House Seed Company created Great White Shark from Super Skunk and White Widow-related genetics. The breeder traditionally lists the ancestry as Super Skunk, Brazilian, and South Indian, with the Brazilian and South Indian components coming through the White Widow genetic foundation. This combination explains the plant’s blend of Skunk sweetness, earthy White-family aromas, strong resin production, and heavy physical effects.
How strong is Great White Shark weed?

Classic breeder information places THC around the mid-teens, while modern examples may test closer to 20% or occasionally higher. Despite appearing modest beside some contemporary high-THC strains, Great White Shark can deliver a strong and long-lasting body effect. Dose and personal tolerance are often more important than comparing THC percentages alone.
What does Great White Shark taste like?

The flavor combines earth, herbs, wood, mild fruit sweetness, pepper, and unmistakable skunky cannabis notes. Myrcene, humulene, and beta-caryophyllene commonly shape the terpene profile. Some phenotypes are sweeter and fruitier, while others emphasize pungent earth and Skunk characteristics.
How long does Great White Shark take to flower?

Indoor flowering normally takes approximately eight to nine weeks, with some growers extending the cycle slightly to increase maturity and resin development. Outdoors, harvest generally arrives around late September or early October in suitable Northern Hemisphere climates. Plant maturity, weather conditions, trichome development, and the desired final effect should guide the exact harvest date.
Final Thoughts on Great White Shark

Great White Shark has survived far longer than most cannabis trends because the underlying breeding still makes sense. Super Skunk contributes vigor, sweetness, density, and unmistakable old-school pungency, while the White Widow side brings resin production, earthy complexity, and the Brazilian and South Indian ancestry that helped define an entire generation of Dutch marijuana genetics. The plant flowers relatively quickly, can produce substantial yields, responds well to canopy training, and finishes with the kind of trichome coverage that made the White family famous.

Its effects also provide a useful reminder that THC percentage is not the only measure of cannabis strength. Great White Shark can begin with surprising mental clarity before developing into a deep, long-lasting physical stone capable of making high doses distinctly sedating. Combined with earthy-skunky flavor, peppery herbs, subtle fruit, and thick resin, that progression gives the strain an identity very different from today’s endless procession of sweet dessert hybrids. For growers and consumers interested in historically important weed with genuine staying power, Great White Shark remains one of the more distinctive classics of the 1990s cannabis breeding era.
